title: One Day Rebirth Dev Log｜We stopped writing game logic. AI now maintains it.
author: Former-Objective-272
selftext:
We’ve been building an indie game called *One Day Loop*, and we hit a pretty familiar wall: AI can generate game code, but it doesn’t maintain systems.

Everything looks fine in isolation — NPC logic, platformer rules, quest flow — all “works”.

But once we integrate everything, the system starts breaking in unpredictable ways.

One small rule change breaks multiple systems.  
AI-generated code becomes hard to modify because it’s not really a system — it’s just fragments.

So we changed everything.

Instead of letting AI write game logic directly, we made it work on **system structure only**.

Now every game system is represented as a **graph**:

* world state
* behavior rules
* event relationships

No more hardcoded gameplay logic. No more scattered if/else design.

Then we built a closed loop:

Graph → AI generates implementation → runs simulation → automatic validation → failures feed back into graph/code → repeat

The key is the simulation layer.

We don’t just “run the game”.  
We run automated simulations designed to break it.

Now AI isn’t just generating code — it keeps iterating until the system behaves correctly under simulation.

We started with a 2D platformer system as a test, and it actually worked:

* levels are graph-driven
* physics rules are structured, not hardcoded
* behavior comes from system constraints
* bugs are caught by simulation instead of humans
* AI fixes issues and re-validates automatically

We barely debug gameplay logic anymore.

The weird shift is this:

Game development stopped being about writing code.

It became about designing systems that can sustain themselves.

Even configs are now graphs, not static data.  
Even narrative logic is a “director system”, not scripts.

If this keeps scaling, we’re no longer just building game content.

We’re building a system that maintains its own game logic.

comments.author: Murder_1337
comments.body: What tool / software are you using? Is this efficient way to code tho? Like does the code actually run well?

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
The game logic is built with Rust + Bevy. It’s actually pretty efficient and works well across platforms.

For rendering / presentation I’m using Godot as a thin layer — mostly just assets and user input scripting, with almost no real gameplay logic in it.

The demo you saw is more of a simulation environment with heavy logging and causal tracking running in real time, so 30 FPS isn’t representative of actual game performance. The final build won’t carry that overhead.

One important part of the setup is that AI + Rust gives very stable execution. In my pipeline, the AI and simulator are tightly coupled for iterative validation. If there are hidden runtime issues at the code level, it breaks the consistency of the AI-driven decision loop — so keeping the core logic in a predictable, deterministic Rust layer is actually critical for the whole system to work.

replies.author: Murder_1337
replies.body: I assume that this is done locally and you have good vram? This is how I envision coding agents but doesn’t seem like it’s there fully yet

replies.author: Former-Objective-272
replies.body:
This simulation system is something I built myself. It exposes a set of “AI skills” as an interface layer, so it can be connected to basically any external AI agent setup or tooling.

So the system itself doesn’t depend on a specific model running locally or requiring heavy VRAM. The heavy lifting is in the simulation + deterministic world logic, while the AI part is just calling into skills and interpreting state transitions.

Right now it’s still in an experimental stage, but the goal is to make the AI layer interchangeable so different agents can plug into the same world simulator.
